For a real-valued random variable, finite expectation implies integrability.
Integrability means that the positive and negative parts have finite sums.
If X is integrable, then E(X) is a finite number.
If Y is integrable, then E(Y) is a finite number.
The sum X+Y is also integrable.
This follows from the triangle inequality for absolute values.
Specifically, |X+Y| is bounded above by |X| plus |Y|.
Since |X| and |Y| have finite expectations, their sum has finite expectation.
Therefore X+Y has finite expectation.
The expectation of X+Y equals the sum of the expectations.
So E(X+Y) is E(X) plus E(Y).
This value is finite because both terms are finite.
No rearrangement issue appears in the standard definition.
The standard definition uses positive and negative parts.
A signed variable has a finite expectation only when both parts are finite.
If either part is infinite, the expectation is not finite in that sense.
Thus the stated finite hypotheses rule out the undefined case.
They also rule out an infinite expectation for the sum.
The answer is therefore negative.
This conclusion holds for discrete random variables as well.
